merneptah.title: The name “Israel” in Egyptian hieroglyphs
merneptah.caption: The Merneptah Stele contains the earliest widely accepted extra-biblical reference to a people called Israel in Canaan.

tel_dan.title: The Tel Dan Stele
tel_dan.caption: This ninth-century BCE Aramaic victory inscription is widely read as referring to the “House of David.”
tel_dan.credit: Geagea, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

black_obelisk.title: The Black Obelisk
black_obelisk.caption: An Assyrian monument depicts tribute associated with Jehu’s kingdom and places the northern kingdom inside wider imperial history.

lachish.title: The Assyrian siege of Lachish
lachish.caption: Sennacherib’s palace reliefs show assault ramps, siege engines, captives and exile from a major Judean city in 701 BCE.
lachish.credit: Mike Peel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cyrus.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
cyrus.caption: The inscription illustrates the wider Persian policy world in which displaced peoples and sanctuaries could be restored. It does not mention Judah directly.
cyrus.credit: Mike Peel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

isaiah_scroll.title: The Great Isaiah Scroll
isaiah_scroll.caption: A nearly complete manuscript of Isaiah from the Second Temple period shows the preservation and transmission of prophetic Scripture.
isaiah_scroll.credit: Public-domain artwork reproduction via Wikimedia Commons

pilate.title: The Pilate inscription
pilate.caption: This Latin inscription independently attests Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect connected with Jesus’ crucifixion.

arch_titus.title: The Arch of Titus relief
arch_titus.caption: Roman triumphal art depicts temple spoils, including the menorah, after Jerusalem’s destruction in 70 CE.
arch_titus.credit: Greg, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

bar_kokhba.title: A Bar Kokhba revolt coin
bar_kokhba.caption: The coin’s slogans about the freedom of Jerusalem reveal the revolt’s national and messianic intensity.
bar_kokhba.credit: IsraelXKV8R, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
